newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Rain slows Yugo harvest, wheat crop forecast holds.
newsitem.headline: Rain slows Yugo harvest, wheat crop forecast holds.

text.p: Rainfalls have slowed down combines throughout Yugoslavia where only some 30 percent of the wheat area has been harvested by now.
Analysts on Tuesday stuck to their earlier wheat forecasts at three million tonnes this year despite lower yields and quality of grain in the areas hit by frequent rains.

"Rainy weather hinders the harvest. The central part of (the country's granary) Vojvodina is under frequent rain and harvest is halted again," said Miroslav Malesevic of the Novi Sad Institute for Wheat.
Harvest continues in the north and north-east part of the country but in the southern part of Serbia combines stopped on Tuesday, he told Reuters from Novi Sad by phone.
"Only some one-third of the 800,000 ha under wheat could have been harvested by now," he added.
Last week rain and hail interrupted harvest in many parts of the country, threatning to reduce yields in those areas by several percent.
"Rain damages the quality of crop and lowers the yield. Grain dampness is on the rise and production cost will go up because the wheat will have to be dried," Malesevic said.
He said the yield on the acreage already harvested was as expected. "It varies a lot depending on cultivation methods and it ranges from below two tonnes to above eight tonnes per ha."
The Institute has provided seeds to some private farms which managed to collect even more than eight tonnes per ha.
"Those areas are very limited and most have yielded around seven tonnes. At the same time, some producers harvested only two or fewer tonnes per ha," he said.
Preliminary official forecasts based on the state of crops on May 31 stands at 2.8 million tonnes with expected yields per ha of around 3.44 tonnes. A new forecast is expected in a few days.

Government officials expect the wheat crop to reach three million tonnes this year. This will meet domestic needs and, weather permitting, will leave some 500,000 tonnes for export, local media quoted them as saying.
Malesevic said the average yield could be around three tonnes per ha. "It may even reach 3.1 or 3.2 tonnes per ha but only thanks to the high yields collected from experimental farms."
One trader, who asked not to be named, said Yugoslavia should export and import wheat on a regular basis and be a permanent wheat trading partner abroad.
"We must be present on the world market and become a reliable partner both in buying and selling wheat...and not only from domestic production... if there is any profit to be made," the trader said.
"But to say before the harvest is over that 500,000 tonnes will be exported is a little too optimistic. I personally have seen fields where the colour of wheat is almost like chocolate."
A wheat export quota was set at 500,000 tonnes this year. -- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 311 4254
